opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think generalization is really the central question, and I like to think about it at a few different levels.

At the most basic level, the textbook version, you have a training distribution and a test distribution, and you assume they're the same. Then generalization means: if I've fit my training data, how well do I do on fresh samples from that same distribution? That's what classical learning theory studies with VC dimension, Rademacher complexity and so on. It's a fine question, but frankly it's the least interesting version, because in the real world the test distribution is almost never the training distribution.

The more interesting kind is generalization to new situations. A child who has learned to pick up cups in their own kitchen can pick up a cup in your kitchen, with different lighting, a different table, a cup they've never seen. That isn't interpolation within a fixed distribution. It's a kind of extrapolation, and it works because the child has learned something about the structure of the world: objects, their 3D shape, how hands interact with them. So for me generalization is closely tied to learning the right representations, ones that capture the causal and physical structure of the world rather than superficial correlations in a dataset.

This is also why I'm a bit skeptical of benchmarks. We collect a dataset, split it into train and test, report a number, and declare progress. But often the model has learned shortcuts that happen to work on that dataset: texture instead of shape, background instead of object. Move it to a slightly different setting and performance collapses. So I'd distinguish "benchmark generalization" from the real thing.

Where does the real thing come from? I think nature gives us a hint. Biological organisms learn from enormous amounts of experience, much of it self-supervised: watching, moving, touching, predicting what happens next. They're embodied, so they can act and see the consequences of their actions. Babies aren't given a million labeled images. They interact with the world, and out of that comes a representation that transfers remarkably well. So I'm quite optimistic about self-supervised learning, learning from video, learning in embodied settings, because those are closer to the conditions under which robust generalization arose in the first place.

And there's one more level: generalization across tasks. Not just a new cup, but a new task you haven't been trained on, using knowledge you already have. That's where you see the power of large pretrained models, and also where they still fall short, especially in the physical world. Being able to talk about picking up a cup is not the same as being able to do it. Closing that gap, connecting perception, action and knowledge so that skills transfer flexibly, is to me the big open problem, and it's what I think about most these days.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, thanks for having me, Pieter. This is a question I think about a lot, and I'll say upfront that I don't think any of us fully understand it.

The classical view, the one I was taught, comes from statistical learning theory. You have a hypothesis class, you have some notion of its capacity, VC dimension and so on, and generalization is about the gap between training error and test error being controlled by the ratio of capacity to the amount of data. That picture is mathematically beautiful, and it's basically useless for explaining what we see with deep networks. These models have far more parameters than training examples, they can memorize random labels perfectly, and yet they generalize. So the classical theory tells you the bound is vacuous, and the experiment tells you it works anyway.

So I've come to think about generalization more the way a biologist or a psychologist might. The real question is: what is the structure of the world, and does the learner have the right inductive biases to exploit it? Convolutional networks worked for vision not because of some clever bound, but because the visual world really is translation-invariant and really is hierarchical, local features composing into larger ones. The architecture encoded a true fact about images. That's generalization through good priors, not through counting parameters.

The second thing I'd say is that we should distinguish between kinds of generalization. There's interpolation, where the test data comes from the same distribution as training data, and honestly I think modern systems do that extraordinarily well. Then there's the harder thing, generalizing to new distributions, new tasks, compositional novelty. A child who has seen a few dogs can recognize a dog in a drawing, from behind, in the snow. That kind of robustness is what I'd call real generalization, and it's where we still fall short, though large-scale pretraining has moved the needle more than I expected.

And that points to the third piece, which is that the data matters enormously. When I look at how children learn, they don't get a labeled dataset. They get a continuous stream of multimodal experience, they move around, they act in the world, and the regularities they pick up are the ones that matter for acting. I suspect a lot of what we call generalization in humans comes from that embodied, active, developmental process, and our systems are only starting to approximate it with sheer scale of passive data.

So if you ask me for a one-line answer: generalization is a match between the learner's biases and the structure of the world, and the deep learning era has taught us that scale and the right data can substitute for a surprising amount of hand-built bias. But I'd be lying if I said we have a theory of it.

astra-6.text:
I think of generalization as the ability to use what you have learned in situations you haven’t encountered before. But the important question is: how different are those new situations from the ones in which you learned?

In the standard machine-learning setup, we train on some examples and test on fresh examples drawn from the same distribution. That is a useful measure, but it captures only part of what we mean by intelligence. If a system recognizes an object against a familiar background, does it still recognize it when the background changes, or when it sees the object from a new viewpoint?

So we have to ask what remains stable as the circumstances change. Learning involves assumptions about that structure—what matters, what can be ignored, and how things relate. Generalization depends on whether those assumptions are appropriate for the new situation. It isn’t a single capability that a system either has or lacks; we need to specify what kind of change we expect it to handle.

sol-6.1.text:
I think generalization is really the central question in machine learning. You observe a finite set of examples, but what you care about is how the system behaves on examples it has never seen. And that immediately raises a question: how are those new examples related to the ones you trained on?

In the standard formulation, training and test examples come from the same distribution. That is a useful starting point, but it captures only part of what we mean by intelligence. In vision, for example, you would like to recognize an object from a new viewpoint, under different lighting, or against an unfamiliar background. Some aspects of the image change, while the identity of the object remains the same.

So generalization depends on having the right inductive biases—the assumptions that allow you to go beyond the observations. The architecture, the learning procedure, and the training data all contribute. The interesting question is which regularities the system has learned: are they relationships that continue to hold in new circumstances, or correlations that happen to work in the training environment?
